analogy: a choose-your-own-adventure book that keeps every path taken
breaks: A reader chooses each path in the book, but in a session log the harness and the user make the forks, every path stays readable to them, and the model sees only the path being followed.

analogy: an alarm clock with a note on the bedside table
breaks: An alarm can ring twice, so the note must make a second waking harmless; and the note says where you left off, not what you were thinking.

analogy: an assembly line with fixed stations
breaks: Each station here is a model call that can still return something unexpected.

analogy: booking a trip
breaks: Some steps cannot be undone, and an email cannot be unsent, so the plan needs one pivot after which nothing is compensated.

analogy: a bookmark
breaks: A bookmark restores only your place; a resumed run must also restore pending approvals and tool state, and some SDKs bring back the conversation alone.

analogy: a bridge that must hold every crossing
breaks: A bridge's loads are roughly independent from one crossing to the next; an agent's failures are not independent across runs, because the same task, tool or prompt can fail the same way each time.

analogy: a bus ticket good for a fixed number of stops
breaks: Every bus company counts a stop the same way. SDKs count steps, turns, graph super-steps and model calls, so the same cap allows a different number of model calls in each.

analogy: casting the lead with the most experienced actor, then trying understudies in the same scenes
breaks: A model does not improve with rehearsal; only the prompt and the evals do.

analogy: a circuit breaker with several settings
breaks: A breaker cuts the current and loses what was in flight; the switch must stop new side effects without losing the log of those already begun.

analogy: a club's door list read top to bottom
breaks: A doorman reads names; a pipeline's rules are code that runs in a fixed order and also read what a call asks to do, and the manager at the door is a callback or a person that the pipeline asks.

analogy: a coat check
breaks: A coat stays the same coat; tokens expire and refresh, and the counter must also know whose coat is whose, because one user's token must never answer another user's request.

analogy: a form at a counter with labelled boxes
breaks: A clerk reads what you wrote and asks what you meant when an answer makes no sense; the SDK checks only that each box holds the right type, so a well-formed but invented value passes and your function must check that it is real.

analogy: a court stenographer's record
breaks: A stenographer's record is final as typed. A run's stream also carries partial deltas that the end event supersedes, so a log that kept every delta would hold text the finished message replaces.

analogy: a dropped phone order
breaks: A restaurant has no order number to look up; an agent's write should carry an idempotency key that the other side can be asked about.

analogy: a driving instructor's dual controls
breaks: The instructor's pedals work whenever pressed; an agent must pause and record that a person took over, or it keeps sending its own input and fights the person for the wheel.

concept: UI as a view of the event log
analogy: an election-results board driven by the official count
breaks: A results board only shows the count; an agent UI can also send events back, such as an approval, which the log then records.

analogy: a flight simulator
breaks: A simulator answers the pilot's controls; a scripted mock replays only what was scripted, so it cannot surprise you the way a real model can.

analogy: a forged memo slipped into the in-tray
breaks: An assistant can phone the director to check a memo, but a model has no way to check who wrote any text in its context, so every input can act as an instruction.

analogy: a hardware store that shelves the common tools and fetches the rest from the back room
breaks: A clerk fetches a tool in a minute for the price of waiting; a deferred tool costs a round trip and the tokens of its definition, and it keeps costing those tokens each turn it stays loaded, so the shelf must hold the tools used most.

analogy: a jelly mould
breaks: A mould forces its shape on whatever is poured in. Most SDKs only check the answer's shape after the model has written it, so an answer that does not fit is rejected or retried, and even constrained decoding lets a refusal or a cut-off answer through. Neither a mould nor a schema can vouch for what is inside: a schema fixes the shape of an answer, never its truth.

analogy: a kitchen ticket rail
breaks: A cook remembers yesterday's orders; a model sees only what its context carries, so the loop resends the context on every call.

analogy: a lab glovebox
breaks: A glovebox keeps things in and does not filter what leaves; our sandbox also decides which network hosts a command may reach, and a determined process can still break out of one that shares the host's kernel.

analogy: describing a room by its labelled objects instead of sending a photo
breaks: Labels can be missing or wrong, so some pages, such as a canvas or a video, still need a screenshot.

analogy: writing the order in the ledger before the courier leaves
breaks: The ledger entry records intent, not success; the result is a second entry, and a missing second entry is the unknown outcome.

analogy: a desk with limited space
breaks: A person can open the drawer and fetch a folder; the model cannot, so only the harness decides what goes on the desk.

analogy: a mailroom that stamps each letter's number and bins duplicates
breaks: The mailroom invents no numbers: the id must come from the sender, such as a webhook's delivery id, or a repeat would get a fresh stamp and slip through.

analogy: a news ticker
breaks: The deltas are provisional; the message at the end is the one that counts.

analogy: a parcel's tracking history
breaks: A span also carries token counts and cost, which a tracking page does not, and a span tree nests steps inside steps where a parcel's history is a flat list.

analogy: passport control, where the officer reads your passport, not what you claim at the desk
breaks: A traveller carries the passport and hands it over; in an agent, your code reads the identity from the signed-in session and hands it to the tool, so the model never carries it and sees it only if your code shows it.

analogy: a patient's chart that travels with them between shifts
breaks: A nurse skims the chart for what matters tonight; your code sends the model the whole session on every call, and the provider bills you for every token of it.

analogy: a play's preview performances before opening night
breaks: A preview audience knows it is a preview; real users are real from the first stage, so the first stage is shadow mode, where the agent proposes and nothing is applied.

analogy: a TV show's "previously on" recap
breaks: A model writes the recap and can drop facts, so the original entries stay in the log and the harness can put any of them back in front of the model.

analogy: firms that contract through a standard purchase order
breaks: A purchase order is filed and forgotten, while an A2A task can stream updates and ask for more input; and a firm vets a supplier before it signs, whereas an Agent Card is unvetted self-description that the calling model reads as prose.

analogy: a raffle ticket stub
breaks: A stub is printed before anyone wins and kept by the holder; an idempotency key must be stored before the call, or a crash loses it and the write can repeat.

analogy: a referee's whistle at each broken rule
breaks: A check knows only the rules you wrote; a game can go wrong in ways no rule names, and a check that holds for the right behaviour may hold for no behaviour at all.

analogy: a bank's second signature on a large payment
breaks: A teller checks the signature against the paper order in front of them. A saved run is text that your storage can change, so the SDK has to compute the signature over the tool name, call id and input, and of the three SDKs here, only the AI SDK documents such a signature, and only when you set a secret.

analogy: a mechanic's service manuals, opened only when that model of car comes in
breaks: A mechanic closes the manual when the car leaves the lift; a skill read into context stays there and costs its tokens in every later request of the run.

analogy: standard shipping containers
breaks: Every port still needs its own crane: each target needs its own adapter behind the same seam, and a seam that fits is proved by a conformance suite, not assumed.

analogy: smoke detectors in several rooms
breaks: A detector only sounds an alarm and leaves the response to a person, while a tripped guardrail can halt the run itself; and no number of detectors makes a building fireproof, as no set of guardrails makes an agent safe.

analogy: a taxi meter that runs on both legs of the trip
breaks: Cached input is billed at a discount; a taxi has no such fare.

analogy: a teaching assistant grading against a rubric
breaks: A judge can be wrong in systematic ways, such as favouring longer answers, so its grades are checked against a person's before they gate anything.

analogy: toll booths that can stop, charge or turn back a car
breaks: A toll booth leaves the car as it is. An interceptor can rewrite the request itself, as if the attendant swapped the driver's destination, so the run records which replacement it used.

analogy: the briefing card a tour guide carries on every tour
breaks: The model cannot ask what the card means, and a changed card breaks the cache.

analogy: traffic cameras that only watch
breaks: A camera that jams cannot close the road, but an observer that throws or never returns can still break a run unless the SDK isolates it and bounds the wait.

analogy: a USB port: one plug shape for many devices
breaks: Plugging in an MCP server is closer to installing software than to plugging in a mouse: the server chooses its tools' names, descriptions and results, and the specification tells clients to treat a tool's annotations as untrusted unless the server is trusted.

analogy: a valet key that moves the car but leaves the boot locked
breaks: A valet key is a real key with fewer powers, held by the attendant; the sandbox never holds the secret at all, and the host adds it at egress.

analogy: a vending machine that hands back your coin with a note
breaks: You read the note and act on it; a model may ignore an error, so the error must say exactly what to try next, and the loop still needs a cap.
